Many analyses start by turning one graph into another: extracting the part that matters, dropping
edge directions, merging nodes that stand for the same thing, combining two data sources, or
deriving a new kind of graph altogether, such as one whose nodes are the edges of the original.
This page covers these transformations.

Almost all of them return a *new* graph and leave the original unchanged, so the original remains
available for comparison. The exceptions are the cleanup methods, such as `simplify()` and
`relabel_nodes()`, which modify the graph in place like the other editing methods (see
[The graph model](graph-model.qmd#methods-modify-the-graph-in-place)).

## Extracting part of a graph

### Subgraphs

[`subgraph()`](../reference/Graph.subgraph.qmd) takes a list of node IDs and returns the *induced*
subgraph: those nodes and every edge among them. Nodes and edges keep their IDs, labels, and
attributes, so results computed on the subgraph can be matched back to the original. A list of IDs
is easy to get from the node table with a Polars filter, here the administrator's faction in the
karate club:

::: {#20f61e0b .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

karate = ec.karate_club()
members = karate.get_node_df().filter(pl.col("faction") == 2)["id"].to_list()
faction = karate.subgraph(members)
faction.count_nodes(), faction.count_edges()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2}
```
(18, 35)
```
:::
:::


The administrator's faction has 18 members and 35 friendships among them. The other 43 of the
club's 78 friendships either lie within the instructor's faction or cross between the two.

[`edge_subgraph()`](../reference/Graph.edge_subgraph.qmd) selects by edges instead, and keeps the
given edges together with their endpoints. This is the way to filter a weighted network by the
strength of its ties. In the *Les Misérables* network, the weight of an edge is the number of
chapters in which two characters appear together. Keeping only the pairs that appear together in
at least five chapters:

::: {#0e0323de .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
miserables = ec.les_miserables()
strong = miserables.get_edge_df().filter(pl.col("weight") >= 5)["id"].to_list()
backbone = miserables.edge_subgraph(strong)
backbone.count_nodes(), backbone.count_edges()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3}
```
(26, 51)
```
:::
:::


Only 51 of the 254 edges, among 26 of the 77 characters, are that strong. Apart from one pair of
minor characters, they form a single component. Taking that component with `subgraph()` and
drawing it shows the core relationships of the novel:

::: {#a3d4854d .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
main = backbone.subgraph(list(backbone.weakly_connected_components()[0]))
main.plot(label_by="label", node_size=10, seed=3, width=700, height=500)
```

### Ego networks

The *ego network* of a node is the subgraph made up of the node, its neighbors, and the edges among
them. It is the basic unit of personal network analysis: who are this person's contacts, and how do
they know each other? [`ego_graph()`](../reference/Graph.ego_graph.qmd) extracts it, and
`radius=` widens it to the neighbors of neighbors and beyond:

::: {#57cf0363 .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
ego = karate.ego_graph(34)
ego.count_nodes(), ego.count_edges(), karate.ego_graph(34, radius=2).count_nodes()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5}
```
(18, 32, 24)
```
:::
:::


The administrator has 17 friends, and with them a neighborhood of 18 members. Within two steps,
the neighborhood grows to 24 of the club's 34 members. With `center=False`, the ego network leaves
out the central node itself, which shows how the contacts are linked without it:

::: {#e657197b .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
alters = karate.ego_graph(34, center=False)
[len(component) for component in alters.weakly_connected_components()]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6}
```
[14, 1, 1, 1]
```
:::
:::


Without the administrator, 14 of the administrator's friends still form one group, while the other
three know none of the rest. Those three depend on the administrator for any connection to the
group, a position that the structural holes measures of [Centrality](centrality.qmd) quantify.
On a directed graph, `mode=` chooses whether the neighborhood follows edges out of the node, into
it, or both, and on a weighted graph the radius is a total edge weight rather than a number of
steps.

## Changing direction

[`to_undirected()`](../reference/Graph.to_undirected.qmd) drops edge directions, which many
algorithms require, and which suits relations whose direction doesn't matter for the question at
hand. When a directed graph has edges in both directions between two nodes, they become a single
undirected edge:

::: {#ba5212a3 .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
votes = ec.wiki_vote()
undirected = votes.to_undirected()
votes.count_edges(), undirected.count_edges()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7}
```
(103689, 100762)
```
:::
:::


The election network has 2,927 pairs of users who voted for each other, and each pair becomes a
single edge. The kept edge is the one that was added first, with its weight and attributes; the
weight of the reverse edge is not added to it, so combine weights beforehand if that matters.

[`to_directed()`](../reference/Graph.to_directed.qmd) goes the other way, and replaces each
undirected edge with a pair of opposite directed edges, so that the karate club's 78 friendships
become 156 directed ties:

::: {#caec325a .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
karate.to_directed().count_edges()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8}
```
156
```
:::
:::


[`reverse()`](../reference/Graph.reverse.qmd) flips the direction of every edge, so that "cites"
becomes "is cited by" and the nodes that a node can reach become the nodes that can reach it. It is
the way to run a forward-only method, such as a traversal, against the direction of the edges.
[`moral_graph()`](../reference/Graph.moral_graph.qmd) is a specialized conversion for Bayesian
networks, which links the parents of each node before dropping the directions (see
[Directed acyclic graphs](dags.qmd)).

## Cleaning up

[Building graphs](building-graphs.qmd#cleaning-up) describes the methods that
remove self-loops and duplicate edges: `remove_selfloops()`, `remove_duplicate_edges()`, and
`simplify()`, which does both. Unlike the transformations on this page, they modify the graph in
place. To keep the original, take a copy first with a subgraph of all the nodes (`limit=None`
lifts the default limit of 1,000 IDs from `get_node_ids()`):

::: {#0d193d9a .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
grqc = ec.ca_grqc()
simple = grqc.subgraph(grqc.get_node_ids(limit=None)).simplify()
grqc.count_edges(), simple.count_edges()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9}
```
(28980, 14484)
```
:::
:::


The co-authorship network records each pair of co-authors twice, once in each direction, so
simplifying the copy roughly halves its edges and leaves the original intact.
[`relabel_nodes()`](../reference/Graph.relabel_nodes.qmd), also in place, renames nodes without
changing their IDs, as described in [The graph model](graph-model.qmd).

## Merging nodes

Two nodes sometimes stand for the same thing: two records of one person, two stops that are really
one station, or two families joined by marriage that act as one. *Contracting* them replaces them
with a single node that has the edges of both.
[`contract_nodes()`](../reference/Graph.contract_nodes.qmd) merges its second node into its first.
In the Florentine families network, the Tornabuoni were close allies of the Medici:

::: {#31496ad5 .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
florentine = ec.florentine_families()
merged = florentine.contract_nodes("Medici", "Tornabuoni", self_loops=False)
merged.count_nodes(), [merged.get_label_from_id(node) for node in merged.get_neighbors("Medici")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10}
```
(14, ['Acciaiuoli', 'Barbadori', 'Ridolfi', 'Albizzi', 'Salviati', 'Guadagni'])
```
:::
:::


The merged Medici node has taken over the Tornabuoni's marriage tie to the Guadagni, while the
tie to the Ridolfi, which both families had, appears only once. The edge between the two merged
nodes would become a self-loop; `self_loops=False` drops it.
[`contracted_edge()`](../reference/Graph.contracted_edge.qmd) does the same but requires the two
nodes to be linked, and [`contract_nodes_multi()`](../reference/Graph.contract_nodes_multi.qmd)
merges a whole list of nodes into the first.

[`quotient_graph()`](../reference/Graph.quotient_graph.qmd) collapses every group of a partition
at once, giving a zoomed-out graph with one node per group and an edge wherever any edge ran
between two groups. Collapsing the karate club by faction:

::: {#120b55f2 .cell execution_count=11}

``` {.python .cell-code}
by_faction = [

]
quotient = karate.quotient_graph(by_faction)
quotient.get_node_df()
```

The quotient nodes are labelled `"block_0"`, `"block_1"`, and so on, in the order of the groups,
and the `members` attribute lists the original nodes of each. Quotient graphs are most useful with
many groups, such as the communities found by a detection method, where they show which groups
are linked to which; [Community detection](communities.qmd) has an example.
[`condensation()`](../reference/Graph.condensation.qmd) is the special case for directed graphs
that collapses each strongly connected component (see [Connectivity and flows](connectivity.qmd)).

## Derived graphs

Some transformations build a different kind of graph from the original.

The *complement* links exactly the pairs that are not linked in the original. A clique in a graph
is an independent set in its complement, so the complement turns problems about one into problems
about the other. [`complement()`](../reference/Graph.complement.qmd) returns it:

::: {#64ddfc43 .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
karate.complement().count_edges()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12}
```
483
```
:::
:::


The complement of the karate club has 483 edges, one for each pair of members who are not friends.

The *line graph* turns edges into nodes: each edge of the original becomes a node, and two nodes
are linked when their edges share an endpoint. This lets any method for nodes be applied to edges,
for example community detection to find overlapping communities, or centrality to find the most
important links. [`line_graph()`](../reference/Graph.line_graph.qmd) labels each new node by the
IDs of the original endpoints, and records the original edge in its attributes:

::: {#3914dc65 .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
line = karate.line_graph()
line.get_node_df().sort("degree", descending=True).head(3)
```

### Spanners

A *spanner* is a sparse subgraph that keeps distances approximately. With a stretch of `t`, the
distance between any two nodes in the spanner is at most `t` times their distance in the original,
so a spanner can stand in for a dense network when approximate distances are enough.
[`transform_with_spanner()`](../reference/Graph.transform_with_spanner.qmd) builds one with a
randomized algorithm:

::: {#546751dd .cell execution_count=16}
``` {.python .cell-code}
jazz = ec.jazz().simplify()
spanner = jazz.transform_with_spanner(stretch=3, seed=1)
(
    spanner.count_edges(),
    jazz.count_edges(),
    round(jazz.mean_distance(), 2),
    round(spanner.mean_distance(), 2),
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16}
```
(381, 2742, 2.24, 3.43)
```
:::
:::


The spanner keeps 381 of the jazz network's 2,742 edges, 14% of them, and the mean distance between
musicians rises from 2.24 steps to 3.43. Every distance at least stays within the guaranteed factor
of three. The construction is fast on graphs of a few thousand edges but slows considerably on
larger ones.

## Combining graphs

### Set operations

Graphs that describe the same nodes can be combined edge by edge, like sets.
[`union()`](../reference/Graph.union.qmd) keeps the edges of both graphs,
[`intersection()`](../reference/Graph.intersection.qmd) the edges they share,
[`difference()`](../reference/Graph.difference.qmd) the edges of the first that are not in the
second, and [`symmetric_difference()`](../reference/Graph.symmetric_difference.qmd) the edges in
exactly one of them. They are the natural tools for comparing snapshots of a network, or for
merging data sources.

These operations match nodes by **ID**, not by label. Two graphs built independently from edge
lists number their nodes in the order they first appear, so the same person can get different IDs
in each. The safe pattern is to build every graph on the same list of nodes, added in the same
order, before adding its edges:

::: {#e4851fde .cell execution_count=17}
``` {.python .cell-code}
people = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cleo", "Dev", "Eli"]


def contacts(edges):
    return ec.Graph().add_nodes(people).add_edges(edges)


def named_edges(graph):
    label = graph.get_label_from_id
    return [(label(source), label(target)) for _, source, target in graph.get_edges_as_tuples()]


march = contacts([("Ana", "Ben"), ("Ben", "Cleo"), ("Cleo", "Dev"), ("Ana", "Cleo")])
june = contacts([("Ana", "Ben"), ("Ben", "Cleo"), ("Dev", "Eli"), ("Cleo", "Eli")])

(
    named_edges(march.intersection(june)),
    named_edges(march.difference(june)),
    named_edges(june.difference(march)),
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17}
```
([('Ana', 'Ben'), ('Ben', 'Cleo')],
 [('Cleo', 'Dev'), ('Ana', 'Cleo')],
 [('Dev', 'Eli'), ('Cleo', 'Eli')])
```
:::
:::


Two contacts lasted from March to June, two ended, and two began. The intersection and the
differences drop nodes that are left without edges, while the union keeps every node of both
graphs. Where both graphs give the same node or edge a label, an attribute, or a weight, `union()`
keeps the value from the graph it is called on; [`compose()`](../reference/Graph.compose.qmd) is
the same operation with the other graph's values taking precedence, which suits applying a batch of
updates to a base network. [`union_all()`](../reference/Graph.union_all.qmd),
[`compose_all()`](../reference/Graph.compose_all.qmd), and [`intersection_all()`](../reference/Graph.intersection_all.qmd)
combine any number of graphs, given as a list, as in `ec.Graph.union_all([march, june])`.

### Side by side

[`disjoint_union()`](../reference/Graph.disjoint_union.qmd) puts two graphs side by side without
merging any nodes. The second graph's IDs are shifted above the first's, and labels that would
clash get a numeric suffix:

``` {.python .cell-code}
pentagon = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(n=5)
pentagon.disjoint_union(pentagon).get_node_df()["label"].to_list()
```

### Products

A *graph product* builds a graph whose nodes are pairs, one node from each factor. The products
differ in which pairs they link. In the *Cartesian product*, two pairs are linked when they agree in
one coordinate and are linked in the other, which builds familiar structures from simple pieces: a
path times a path is a grid, a cycle times a cycle is a torus, and repeated products of a single
edge are hypercubes:

::: {#159f0de7 .cell execution_count=20}
``` {.python .cell-code}
grid = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(n=3).cartesian_product(ec.Graph().add_path_graph(n=4))
edge = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(n=2)
cube = edge.cartesian_product(edge).cartesian_product(edge)

(
    grid.is_isomorphic(ec.Graph().add_grid_2d(rows=3, cols=4)),
    cube.is_isomorphic(ec.Graph().add_hypercube_graph(3)),
    grid.get_node_df()["label"].head(4).to_list(),
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20}
```
(True, True, ['(1, 1)', '(1, 2)', '(1, 3)', '(1, 4)'])
```
:::
:::

cylinder, a ring of rings:

``` {.python .cell-code}
cylinder.plot(show_labels=False, seed=2, width=500, height=400)
```

```{=html}
    try{var d=JSON.parse(raw)}catch(e){return}
    var h='';
    for(var k in d){
      var v=d[k];
      if(typeof v==='number'&&!Number.isInteger(v)) v=v.toFixed(4);
      h+='<div><b>'+k+'</b>: '+v+'</div>';
    }
    if(!h) return;
    tip.innerHTML=h;tip.style.display='block';
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  }
  svg.addEventListener('mouseover',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge')) show(t,ev);
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mousemove',function(ev){
    var r=svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    tip.style.left=(ev.clientX-r.left+12)+'px';
    tip.style.top=(ev.clientY-r.top-10)+'px';
  });
  svg.addEventListener('mouseout',function(ev){
    var t=ev.target;
    if(t.hasAttribute('data-node')||t.hasAttribute('data-edge'))
      tip.style.display='none';
  });
})();
</script>
```

Products also model systems made of independent parts: the joint states of two machines, each of
which changes state one step at a time, form the Cartesian product of their state graphs. The other
products are these:

| Method | Two pairs `(g, h)` and `(g', h')` are linked when |
|---|---|
| [`cartesian_product()`](../reference/Graph.cartesian_product.qmd) | one coordinate is equal and the other is linked |
| [`tensor_product()`](../reference/Graph.tensor_product.qmd) | both coordinates are linked |
| [`strong_product()`](../reference/Graph.strong_product.qmd) | either of the above |
| [`lexicographic_product()`](../reference/Graph.lexicographic_product.qmd) | `g` and `g'` are linked, or `g = g'` and `h` and `h'` are linked |
| [`modular_product()`](../reference/Graph.modular_product.qmd) | both coordinates are linked, or neither is (used to find common subgraphs) |
| [`corona_product()`](../reference/Graph.corona_product.qmd) | a copy of the second graph is attached to every node of the first |
| [`rooted_product()`](../reference/Graph.rooted_product.qmd) | a copy of a rooted graph hangs from every node of the first |
